title: Myrrha
titleEn: Myrrha and the Nurse — Metamorphoses X.298–413
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The poet warns daughters and parents away from the story and congratulates his own part of the world for lying far from it, then follows Myrrha as she argues with her desire for her father Cinyras — from the animals that mate without offence to the laws she calls envious — while Cinyras, pressing her about suitors, mistakes her tears for a girl's shyness. Sleepless and finding no relief but death, she ties her sash to the top of the doorpost for a noose and is caught in time by her old nurse, who guesses that she is in love and promises help, and is still pressing her for the rest when the part ends.

sentences.t:
Editus hac ille est, qui, si sine prole fuisset,
inter felices Cinyras potuisset haberi.
sentences.l: Brought forth from her was he who, if he had been without offspring, could have been reckoned among the happy — Cinyras.
sentences.i: From her was born Cinyras, who, had he been childless, might have been counted among the fortunate.
sentences.n: A past contrary-to-fact condition: si ... fuisset with potuisset haberi, “if he had been ..., he could have been reckoned.” haberi is the passive infinitive, “to be held, counted.” Ovid holds the name Cinyras back into the second line, inside the relative clause and after the verdict on him has begun; the literal puts it last of all, which is the nearest English can come. hac is an ablative of source, “from this woman,” pointing back before this part opens.

sentences.t: Dira canam: procul hinc natae, procul este parentes!
sentences.l: Dreadful things shall I sing: far from here, daughters — far off be, parents!
sentences.i: I shall sing of horrors: away from here, daughters — away, parents!
sentences.n: canam is future, “I shall sing”; dira is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, “dreadful things.” este is the plural imperative of esse, “be,” and it governs both halves: daughters and parents alike are told to stand well off. Magnus prints parentes, a vocative plural addressing the parents; some editions print parente, which would be an ablative after procul, “far from a parent.”

sentences.t:
Aut, mea si vestras mulcebunt carmina mentes,
desit in hac mihi parte fides, nec credite factum,
vel, si credetis, facti quoque credite poenam.
sentences.l: Or, if my songs shall charm your minds, let belief in me be wanting in this part, and do not believe the deed [was done]; or, if you will believe it, believe also the punishment of the deed.
sentences.i: Or, if my song does win you over, let me not be believed in this one part: do not believe the deed was ever done — or, if you do believe it, believe as well in the punishment that followed.
sentences.n: desit is a jussive subjunctive of desum, “let it be wanting.” mihi is the dative of the person concerned, and fides here is the credit an audience gives a poet, not good faith — which is why the literal renders the two together as “belief in me.” credite is a plural imperative and credetis a future indicative — “do not believe ... if you will believe.” factum is the participle used as a noun, “the deed”; “[was done]” is supplied in the literal for English. The quoque in facti quoque is the adverb “also,” not the ablative of qui, a distinction worth watching wherever the word appears.

sentences.t:
Si tamen admissum sinit hoc natura videri,
gentibus Ismariis et nostro gratulor orbi,
gratulor huic terrae, quod abest regionibus illis,
quae tantum genuere nefas.
sentences.l: If nevertheless nature allows this deed to be looked upon, I congratulate the Ismarian peoples and our part of the world; I congratulate this land, because it lies far from those regions which begot so great an abomination.
sentences.i: If nature does allow such a deed to be looked at, then I offer my congratulations to the peoples of Ismarus and to our own quarter of the world — congratulations to this land, for lying far from the regions that bred so monstrous a thing.
sentences.n: gratulor takes the dative: gentibus, orbi and terrae are all datives of the person congratulated. genuere is the poetic third-person plural perfect, -ere for -erunt (genuerunt) — a shortened form, not a different tense, and one to expect again. Ismarus is a mountain in Thrace, so “Ismarian” stands for “Thracian.” quod abest gives the ground of the congratulation, “because it is away from.”

sentences.t:
Sit dives amomo
cinnamaque costumque suum sudataque ligno
tura ferat floresque alios Panchaia tellus,
dum ferat et murram: tanti nova non fuit arbor.
sentences.l: Let the Panchaian land be rich in amomum, and let it bear cinnamon and its own costus and frankincense sweated out of the wood and other flowers — provided that it bear myrrh too: the new tree was not worth so much.
sentences.i: Let Panchaia be rich in amomum; let it bear cinnamon and its own costus and the incense that sweats from the wood, and other flowers besides — so long as it bears myrrh as well: the new tree was not worth the price.
sentences.n: Sit and ferat are jussive subjunctives, “let it be,” “let it bear,” and their subject Panchaia tellus is held back to the end of its line. dives takes the ablative amomo, “rich in amomum.” dum ferat is a proviso clause, “provided that it bear.” sudata ligno, “sweated out of the wood,” is the resin of the incense tree. tanti is a genitive of value, “worth so much”; nova arbor, “the new tree,” takes up the murram standing earlier in this same line 310, and the poet's verdict is that the spice did not repay what produced it. Panchaia is the fabled spice island off Arabia.

sentences.t:
Ipse negat nocuisse tibi sua tela Cupido,
Myrrha, facesque suas a crimine vindicat isto.
sentences.l: Cupid himself denies that his own weapons harmed you, Myrrha, and clears his torches of that crime of yours.
sentences.i: Cupid himself denies that his arrows wounded you, Myrrha; he clears his own torches of that charge against you.
sentences.n: An apostrophe: the poet turns away from his audience to address Myrrha directly, and goes on addressing her for several lines. negat ... nocuisse is indirect statement with sua tela as its accusative subject, “denies that his weapons harmed.” vindicare a crimine is the idiom for clearing someone of a charge, “to claim away from.” isto is the demonstrative of the second person, “that crime there, the one attached to you.”

sentences.t:
Stipite te Stygio tumidisque adflavit echidnis
e tribus una soror.
sentences.l: With a Stygian brand and with swollen vipers one out of the three sisters breathed upon you.
sentences.i: It was one of the three Furies who breathed upon you with her torch out of the Styx and her swollen vipers.
sentences.n: The subject, e tribus una soror, “one sister out of the three,” is held to the very end of the sentence; the three sisters are the Furies. adflavit governs the accusative te and the ablatives of means stipite and echidnis, “breathed on you with.” echidna is a Greek word for a viper, here the snakes in a Fury's hair. Stygius is “of the Styx,” the river of the underworld.

sentences.t:
Scelus est odisse parentem:
hic amor est odio maius scelus.
sentences.l: It is a crime to hate a parent: this love is a crime greater than hatred.
sentences.i: To hate a parent is a crime; this love is a worse crime than hatred.
sentences.n: odisse is perfect in form but present in meaning, “to hate”; the infinitive is the subject of est, “to hate is a crime.” odio is an ablative of comparison after maius, “greater than hatred,” where English needs “than.” The parent meant is Cinyras, and the point of the couplet is that Myrrha has found the one thing worse than the worst thing.

sentences.t:
Undique lecti
te cupiunt proceres, totoque oriente iuventus
ad thalami certamen adest.
sentences.l: Nobles picked from every quarter desire you, and out of the whole East the young manhood is on hand for the contest of the marriage-chamber.
sentences.i: Chosen princes from every quarter want you, and from all the East the young men have come to compete for your hand.
sentences.n: lecti is the perfect participle of lego, “chosen, picked out,” agreeing with proceres. iuventus is a collective singular, “the young men,” and takes the singular verb adest. toto oriente is an ablative, “from the whole East.” thalami is a genitive with certamen: the thalamus is the marriage-chamber, so the contest is for the marriage. The apostrophe continues — te is still Myrrha.

sentences.t:
Ex omnibus unum
elige, Myrrha, virum: dum ne sit in omnibus unus.
sentences.l: Out of them all choose one man, Myrrha: provided only that one man be not among them all.
sentences.i: Choose one husband from them all, Myrrha — so long as one man is not among them.
sentences.n: dum ne with the subjunctive sit is a negative proviso, “provided only that ... not.” The line turns on the repetitions unum ... unus and omnibus ... omnibus: choose one out of all, so long as one of all is excluded. The one excluded is Cinyras, whom the poet pointedly does not name. vir means both “man” and “husband”; the literal keeps “man,” the idiomatic takes “husband.”

sentences.t:
Illa quidem sentit foedoque repugnat amori
et secum “quo mente feror? quid molior?” inquit:
sentences.l: She indeed feels it and fights against the foul love, and to herself she says: “Whither am I borne in mind? What am I contriving?”
sentences.i: She does feel it, and she fights back against the loathsome love, and says to herself: “Where am I being carried, in my mind? What am I setting in motion?”
sentences.n: repugnat takes the dative, foedo ... amori, “fights against the foul love”; both words stand inside line 319. foedus is a hard word — “filthy, foul” — and it is the narrator's word here, not yet hers. feror is passive, “I am carried,” with mente an ablative of respect, “in mind.” molior is deponent: passive in form, active in meaning, “I am contriving, setting in motion.”

sentences.t:
“di, precor, et pietas sacrataque iura parentum,
hoc prohibete nefas scelerique resistite nostro, —
si tamen hoc scelus est.
sentences.l: “Gods, I pray, and duty, and the hallowed rights of parents, forbid this abomination and withstand our crime — if, though, this is a crime.
sentences.i: “Gods — I beg you — and family duty, and the sacred claims that parents have: forbid this horror, stand in the way of my crime — if it is a crime after all.
sentences.n: The vocatives are di, pietas and iura, and the imperatives prohibete and resistite are plural to match all three. resistite takes the dative, scelerique ... nostro, “withstand our crime”; nostro is the plural of modesty for “my,” which is why the idiomatic reads “my crime.” pietas is the Roman name for the duty owed to family and gods, and “duty” is a thin English for it. The dash and the following si tamen turn the prayer against itself the moment it is out of her mouth.

sentences.t:
Sed enim damnare negatur
hanc venerem pietas, coeuntque animalia nullo
cetera delicto.
sentences.l: But in truth duty is said not to condemn this love, and the rest of the animals couple with no offence.
sentences.i: But then — family duty is said not to condemn this kind of love, and the other animals mate with no wrongdoing at all.
sentences.n: negatur with an infinitive is a personal passive, “is said not to”: pietas is the nominative subject both of negatur and of damnare, so the sense is “duty is said not to condemn,” not “it is denied to duty.” venus here is sexual love. nullo ... delicto is an ablative of attendant circumstance, “with no offence,” and cetera animalia is “the rest of the animals,” meaning all but human beings. Magnus prints delicto; some editions print dilectu, “in their choosing,” which shifts the point from guilt to selection.

sentences.t:
Nec habetur turpe iuvencae
ferre patrem tergo, fit equo sua filia coniunx,
sentences.l: Nor is it counted shameful for a heifer to carry her father on her back; for a horse his own daughter becomes his mate,
sentences.i: There is nothing shameful in a heifer's carrying her father on her back; a stallion's own daughter becomes his mate,
sentences.n: turpe is a neuter predicate with the impersonal habetur, “it is held shameful,” and the infinitive ferre is its subject. iuvencae is a dative of the person concerned, “for a heifer,” and equo is likewise dative, “for a horse.” tergo is an ablative of place, “on her back.” This begins the animal argument, a rising series of four examples — heifer, horse, goat, bird — which Myrrha herself throws over at line 335 with Quid in ista revolvor?

sentences.t:
quasque creavit init pecudes caper, ipsaque, cuius
semine concepta est, ex illo concipit ales.
sentences.l: and the he-goat enters the flocks that he himself begot; and the bird herself, from whose seed she was conceived, conceives from that same one.
sentences.i: the he-goat mates with the flock he fathered; and the bird conceives by the very male from whose seed she was conceived.
sentences.n: quas ... pecudes has the antecedent drawn inside its own relative clause — “the flocks which he begot” — a normal Latin arrangement that English has to unpick. init is from ineo, “go into,” the plain word for an animal mounting. ales is feminine here, “the female bird,” and is the subject of concipit; cuius semine and ex illo both point to the male that fathered her. Ovid sets concepta est and concipit side by side to make the circle audible.

sentences.t:
Felices, quibus ista licent! Humana malignas
cura dedit leges, et quod natura remittit,
invida iura negant.
sentences.l: Happy those for whom such things are allowed! Human care has made grudging laws, and what nature allows, envious statutes deny.
sentences.i: Fortunate, the creatures that are permitted such things! It is human anxiety that framed these spiteful laws; what nature permits, jealous law forbids.
sentences.n: licent is plural, and its subject is the neuter plural ista, “such things” — the animal matings just listed; quibus is the dative of those permitted, “for whom they are allowed.” licet is impersonal only where no nominative subject stands beside it, and here one does. The adjectives humana and malignas close line 329 and their nouns cura and leges follow in 330, interlocked across the line-end — humana with cura, malignas with leges. malignas and invida are Myrrha's own words for the laws and they carry resentment — “grudging,” “envious” — and both layers keep that.

sentences.t:
Gentes tamen esse feruntur,
in quibus et nato genetrix et nata parenti
iungitur, ut pietas geminato crescat amore.
sentences.l: Yet nations are reported to exist in which both the mother is joined to her son and the daughter to her parent, so that duty may grow with love doubled.
sentences.i: Still, there are said to be peoples where mother is joined with son and daughter with father, so that family love is doubled and duty grows by it.
sentences.n: feruntur esse is a nominative-and-infinitive, “are said to be”: the Latin marks the claim as hearsay and does not vouch for it. nato and parenti are datives after iungitur, which stays singular although it serves two subjects, genetrix and nata. parens is unmarked for sex, simply “parent,” and it is the pairing with nato genetrix that fixes the parent here as the father: the literal keeps “parent,” which is the word, and the idiomatic gives “father,” which is the sense. ut ... crescat is a purpose clause with the subjunctive, “so that it may grow,” and geminato ... amore is an ablative, “by a doubled love.” Magnus prints ut ... crescat; some editions print et ... crescit, which would make it a further statement rather than a purpose.

sentences.t:
Me miseram, quod non nasci mihi contigit illic,
fortunaque loci laedor! — Quid in ista revolvor?
sentences.l: Wretched me — because it did not fall to me to be born there, and I am injured by the luck of my birthplace! — Why am I rolling back into these thoughts?
sentences.i: Poor me, that I did not happen to be born there — I am wronged by the accident of where I was born! — Why do I keep going back over this?
sentences.n: Me miseram is an accusative of exclamation, “wretched me,” standing outside any construction. contigit is impersonal with the dative mihi and the infinitive nasci, “it fell to my lot to be born.” fortuna loci is an ablative of means with the passive laedor, “I am harmed by.” revolvor is passive in form but reflexive in force, “I roll myself back”: the image is of unrolling a scroll to the same place again. The dash marks her catching herself in the act.

sentences.l: Forbidden hopes, go away! He is worthy to be loved — but as a father. — And so, if I were not great Cinyras' daughter, I could lie with Cinyras;
sentences.i: Away with you, forbidden hopes! He deserves to be loved — but as a father. — So then: if I were not the daughter of great Cinyras, I could go to bed with Cinyras.
sentences.n: Spes interdictae is a vocative plural addressed to her own hopes, with the imperative discedite. dignus amari puts a passive infinitive after dignus, a poetic construction where prose would write dignus qui ametur, “worthy to be loved.” si ... non essem ... possem is a present contrary-to-fact condition, both verbs imperfect subjunctive: “if I were not, I could.” The name stands twice in succession in different cases — genitive Cinyrae, “daughter of Cinyras,” then dative Cinyrae after concumbere, “lie with Cinyras” — the same man in the two roles she cannot hold at once.

sentences.t:
nunc quia iam meus est, non est meus, ipsaque damno
est mihi proximitas: aliena potentior essem.
sentences.l: as it is, because he is already mine, he is not mine, and the very nearness [of blood] is a loss to me: were I a stranger, I should be stronger.
sentences.i: As things stand, because he is already mine he is not mine, and it is the very closeness that does me harm: if I were no relation, I should be in a stronger position.
sentences.n: damno est mihi is the double dative: damno a dative of effect, mihi a dative of the person concerned — “it is for a loss to me.” proximitas, “nearness,” is the nominative subject and means nearness of blood; “[of blood]” is supplied in the literal. aliena is nominative feminine agreeing with the unexpressed “I” — a woman outside the family — and essem is the imperfect subjunctive continuing the contrary-to-fact thought. The turn on meus est / non est meus is the pivot of the whole speech.

sentences.t:
Ire libet procul hinc patriaeque relinquere fines,
dum scelus effugiam.
sentences.l: It is pleasing [to me] to go far from here and to leave the bounds of my native land, so long as I may escape the crime.
sentences.i: I want to go far from here and leave my country's borders behind, if only that lets me escape the crime.
sentences.n: libet is impersonal, “it is pleasing,” with the infinitives ire and relinquere as its subject; the person pleased is left unexpressed in the Latin, and “[to me]” is supplied in the literal. dum with the subjunctive effugiam is a proviso, “provided that I escape,” not the temporal “while”; the poet used the same proviso construction at line 310, dum ferat et murram.

sentences.t:
Retinet malus ardor amantem,
ut praesens spectem Cinyram tangamque loquarque
osculaque admoveam, si nil conceditur ultra.
sentences.l: An evil burning holds back the one who loves, so that, present with him, I may look at Cinyras and touch and speak and set kisses on him — if nothing beyond is granted.
sentences.i: But a wicked passion holds the lover back, so that I may be near him and look at Cinyras and touch him and talk with him and kiss him, if nothing more is allowed me.
sentences.n: amantem is a present participle used as a noun, “the one loving”: she speaks of herself in the third person before slipping back into the first with spectem. ut ... spectem, tangam, loquar, admoveam is a purpose clause with four subjunctives strung together by -que, and loquar is deponent, active in meaning. conceditur is passive with nil as its subject, “if nothing is granted.” Magnus prints amantem, “the lover”; some editions print euntem, “the one going,” which would tie the line back to the ire of line 341.

sentences.t:
Ultra autem spectare aliquid potes, impia virgo?
Et quot confundas et iura et nomina, sentis!
sentences.l: But can you look to something beyond, unholy girl? And you feel how many rights and how many names you are confounding!
sentences.i: But can you look for something more than that, you unholy girl? And you know how many claims and titles you are throwing into confusion!
sentences.n: She rounds on herself in the second person: impia virgo is a vocative, and impius is the word for failing in the duty owed to family and gods — “unholy, undutiful,” the exact opposite of the pietas she prayed to. quot ... confundas is an indirect question after sentis, which is why the verb is subjunctive; English renders it with an indicative. The doubled et ... et is “both ... and,” and sentis is held to the last word for the sting.

sentences.t:
Tune eris et matris paelex et adultera patris?
Tune soror nati genetrixque vocabere fratris?
sentences.l: Will you be both your mother's rival-mistress and your father's adulteress? Will you be called your son's sister and your brother's mother?
sentences.i: Will you be your mother's rival in his bed and your father's adulteress? Will you be called your son's sister and your brother's mother?
sentences.n: The -ne of Tune is the interrogative particle fastened to tu, and its repetition throws the weight onto the person: “you — is it you who will ...?” paelex is a hard word, the mistress who displaces a wife, and Myrrha uses it of herself without softening. vocabere is a second-person future passive, an alternative form for vocaberis, “you will be called.” The four genitives — matris, patris, nati, fratris — name in order the relationships the act would collapse into one another.

sentences.t:
Nec metues atro crinitas angue sorores,
quas facibus saevis oculos atque ora petentes
noxia corda vident?
sentences.l: And will you not fear the sisters haired with black snake, whom guilty hearts see coming at their eyes and faces with savage torches?
sentences.i: And will you not fear the sisters whose hair is black snakes, whom guilty hearts see making for their eyes and faces with cruel torches?
sentences.n: sorores is the Furies again, as at line 314. crinitas, “haired,” takes the ablative atro ... angue, “with black snake,” the singular used collectively for the whole nest. quas is the object of vident and at the same time the subject-accusative of the participle petentes, “whom [hearts] see attacking,” with oculos atque ora as the participle's own objects. noxia corda, “guilty hearts,” is the subject: the Furies are seen by those who have earned them.

sentences.t:
At tu, dum corpore non es
passa nefas, animo ne concipe, neve potentis
concubitu vetito naturae pollue foedus.
sentences.l: But you, so long as you have not undergone the abomination in body, do not conceive it in mind, and do not with forbidden coupling defile the compact of mighty nature.
sentences.i: But while your body is still clear of the horror, do not entertain it in your mind either — do not defile the covenant of mighty nature with a forbidden union.
sentences.n: passa es is the perfect of the deponent patior: passive in form, active in meaning, “you have suffered, undergone.” ne concipe and neve ... pollue are negative commands with the plain imperative, a poetic construction where prose would use noli or ne with the subjunctive. potentis ... naturae is a genitive with foedus, adjective and noun split across the line-end — potentis closes line 352 and naturae stands in 353. concubitu vetito is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Velle puta: res ipsa vetat. Pius ille memorque est
moris — et o vellem similis furor esset in illo!”
sentences.l: Suppose that you do wish it: the fact itself forbids. He is dutiful and mindful of custom — and oh, I should wish a like madness were in him!”
sentences.i: Suppose you did want it — the thing itself forbids. He is a dutiful man and keeps to custom. And oh, I wish the same madness were in him!”
sentences.n: Velle puta is an imperative with a bare infinitive, “suppose [yourself] to want it.” memor takes the genitive moris, “mindful of custom,” and the noun is held over to the start of line 355, split from its adjective across the line-end. vellem is a wishing imperfect subjunctive, “I could wish,” and esset the imperfect subjunctive of an unfulfilled wish, “were it in him.” pius is the very word she turned against herself as impia at line 345: the father has the duty she has lost. The speech ends by wishing away everything it has just argued.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, at Cinyras, quem copia digna procorum,
quid faciat, dubitare facit, scitatur ab ipsa
nominibus dictis, cuius velit esse mariti.
sentences.l: She had spoken; but Cinyras — whom a fitting abundance of suitors makes hesitate what he is to do — asks the girl herself, once the names have been recited, of which husband she wishes to be.
sentences.i: She had finished. But Cinyras, whom the crowd of worthy suitors leaves unsure what to do, asks the girl herself, once he has read out the names, which of them she wants for a husband.
sentences.n: Dixerat is pluperfect, “she had spoken,” the standard way of marking that a speech is over. quid faciat is an indirect deliberative question inside the relative clause — “what he is to do,” not “what he is doing” — with the subjunctive, and dubitare facit is “makes [him] hesitate.” nominibus dictis is an ablative absolute, “the names having been spoken,” which English turns into a clause. cuius ... mariti is a predicate genitive after esse, “to be of which husband,” i.e. whose wife she wants to be, with velit subjunctive in an indirect question. scitatur is deponent, active in meaning.

sentences.t:
Illa silet primo, patriisque in vultibus haerens
aestuat et tepido suffundit lumina rore.
sentences.l: She is silent at first, and, fixed upon her father's face, she burns and suffuses her eyes with warm dew.
sentences.i: At first she says nothing; her eyes fixed on her father's face, she burns, and warm tears well up over them.
sentences.n: primo is the adverb, “at first.” patriis ... vultibus is a poetic plural for the single face, governed by in with haerens, “clinging to, fixed on.” aestuat is the verb of boiling water and of fever alike; here it is the heat of her feeling. tepido ... rore, “with warm dew,” is Ovid's periphrasis for tears and is an ablative of means with suffundit; lumina, “lights,” is the poetic word for eyes.

sentences.t:
Virginei Cinyras haec credens esse timoris,
flere vetat siccatque genas atque oscula iungit.
sentences.l: Cinyras, believing these things to belong to a girl's fear, forbids her to weep, and dries her cheeks, and joins kisses to hers.
sentences.i: Cinyras, taking all this for a girl's nervousness, tells her not to cry, dries her cheeks, and kisses her.
sentences.n: virginei ... timoris is a predicate genitive of characteristic after esse, “to be [a mark] of maidenly fear,” with adjective and noun pushed to the two ends of line 361 and the whole clause between them. credens ... esse is indirect statement with haec as its accusative subject. vetat takes a plain infinitive, flere, “forbids to weep.” oscula iungere is the ordinary phrase for kissing, “to join kisses.” He reads her tears as nothing worse than a bride's nerves.

sentences.t:
Myrrha datis nimium gaudet: consultaque, qualem
optet habere virum, “similem tibi” dixit.
sentences.l: Myrrha rejoices too much in what has been given; and, asked what sort of husband she would wish to have, she said “One like you.”
sentences.i: Myrrha takes too much pleasure in what she is given; and, asked what sort of husband she would wish to have, she said: “One like you.”
sentences.n: datis is a perfect participle used as a neuter plural noun, “the things given,” in the ablative after gaudet, which takes an ablative of cause. consulta is the perfect participle agreeing with Myrrha, “having been consulted.” qualem ... optet habere virum is an indirect question with the subjunctive, “what sort of husband she would wish to have.” gaudet is present and dixit perfect within one sentence: this part alternates historic present and perfect repeatedly, and both layers keep the shift rather than levelling it.

sentences.t:
At ille
non intellectam vocem conlaudat et “esto
tam pia semper” ait.
sentences.l: But he warmly praises the utterance he has not understood, and says: “Be always so dutiful.”
sentences.i: But he praises warmly the words he has not understood, and says, “Always be as dutiful as that.”
sentences.n: non intellectam is a perfect passive participle attached straight to vocem, “the utterance not understood,” where English wants a relative clause. conlaudat keeps the edition's older unassimilated spelling for collaudat; the con- prefix intensifies, hence “praise warmly.” esto is the future imperative of esse, “be — and go on being,” which suits an instruction meant to hold for life. pia is the adjective of pietas: the father hands his daughter the very word she has been arguing with.

sentences.t:
Pietatis nomine dicto
demisit vultus sceleris sibi conscia virgo.
sentences.l: The name of duty having been spoken, the girl, aware in herself of crime, cast down her face.
sentences.i: At the word “duty,” the girl, knowing her own guilt, dropped her eyes.
sentences.n: Pietatis nomine dicto is an ablative absolute, “the name of duty having been spoken,” picking up the pia standing earlier in this same line 366. conscia takes the genitive of the thing known, sceleris, and the dative of the person, sibi — “aware to herself of crime.” demisit vultus keeps the poetic plural for the one face, and the perfect breaks the run of presents before it — conlaudat and ait at lines 365 and 366.

sentences.t:
Noctis erat medium, curasque et corpora somnus
solverat.
sentences.l: It was the middle of the night, and sleep had loosed both cares and bodies.
sentences.i: It was midnight, and sleep had unstrung men's cares and their bodies alike.
sentences.n: medium is a neuter noun, “the middle,” with the genitive noctis: “it was night's middle.” solverat is pluperfect, “had loosened,” and takes two objects of quite different kinds, curas and corpora — anxieties and bodies together under one verb, a compression Latin allows and English resists.

sentences.t:
At virgo Cinyreia pervigil igni
carpitur indomito furiosaque vota retractat.
sentences.l: But the Cinyrean girl, wakeful all night, is plucked at by an untamed fire and goes back over her frenzied prayers.
sentences.i: But Cinyras's daughter lies awake and is worn away by an untamable fire, turning her frantic wishes over and over.
sentences.n: Cinyreia is a Greek-style patronymic adjective, “Cinyras's,” where Latin prose would use a genitive. pervigil is an adjective, “awake right through,” not a verb. carpitur is passive, “she is plucked at, worn away,” with igni ... indomito an ablative of means split across the line-end: igni closes line 369 and indomito stands in 370. retractat is “handles again, goes back over,” and vota are the things she has prayed for.

sentences.t:
Et modo desperat, modo vult temptare, pudetque
et cupit, et, quid agat, non invenit.
sentences.l: And now she despairs, now she wants to make the attempt; and it shames her, and she desires; and she does not find what she is to do.
sentences.i: One moment she gives up, the next she wants to try; shame takes her, then longing; and she cannot find what to do.
sentences.n: modo ... modo is “now ... now,” marking the swing back and forth. pudet is impersonal — “it causes shame,” with the person ashamed in the accusative and here left unexpressed — set immediately beside the ordinary personal cupit, “she desires,” so the Latin changes construction inside one clause; the literal keeps both, “it shames her, and she desires.” quid agat is an indirect deliberative question with the subjunctive, “what she is to do,” not “what she is doing.”

sentences.t:
Utque securi
saucia trabs ingens, ubi plaga novissima restat,
quo cadat, in dubio est omnique a parte timetur:
sentences.l: And as a huge trunk gashed by the axe, when the last stroke is still to come, is in doubt where it is to fall and is feared from every quarter:
sentences.i: And as a great tree-trunk cut into by the axe, with one last blow still to come, hangs uncertain which way it will drop, and is feared on every side —
sentences.n: Utque opens a formal simile whose sic answers at the start of line 375. securi is the ablative of securis, “axe,” an ablative of means with saucia, “wounded, gashed.” novissima is the superlative of novus in its Latin sense of “last, latest,” not “newest.” quo cadat is an indirect deliberative question with the subjunctive, “where it is to fall,” standing as the content of in dubio est. timetur is passive with trabs still its subject, “it is feared,” and omni a parte is “from every quarter.”

sentences.t:
sic animus vario labefactus vulnere nutat
huc levis atque illuc momentaque sumit utroque.
sentences.l: so her mind, made unsteady by wound upon wound, nods this way and that, easily moved, and takes its impulses in either direction.
sentences.i: so her mind, unsettled by blow after blow, tips this way and that, easily swayed, and gathers momentum first one way, then the other.
sentences.n: sic answers the Utque of line 372 and completes the simile. labefactus is a perfect participle, “made to totter,” with vario ... vulnere an ablative of means in which the singular stands for repeated blows, “by wound after wound.” levis is nominative and agrees with animus, so it describes the mind and not the motion — “light, easily moved”; both layers give it to the mind. momenta are the impulses that tip a balance, and utroque is the adverb, “in both directions.”

sentences.t:
Nec modus aut requies, nisi mors, reperitur amoris.
Mors placet.
sentences.l: Nor is any limit or rest of her love found, except death. Death pleases her.
sentences.i: There is no limit to her love and no rest from it, except death. She settles on death.
sentences.n: amoris is a genitive depending on both modus and requies, “a limit or a rest of love,” and it is held to the very end of the line, after the parenthetic nisi mors has interrupted. reperitur is passive, “is found,” with modus and requies as its subjects. placet is the ordinary Latin verb of a resolution taken, “it is decided on,” and the two-word sentence Mors placet is where the long deliberation stops. The literal keeps the transparent surface of the verb, “Death pleases her”; the idiomatic carries the resolution, “She settles on death.”

sentences.t:
Erigitur laqueoque innectere fauces
destinat et zona summo de poste revincta
“care vale Cinyra causamque intellege mortis!”
dixit et aptabat pallenti vincula collo.
sentences.l: She raises herself up and resolves to knot her throat in a noose; and, with her sash tied fast to the top of the doorpost, she said “Dear Cinyras, farewell — and understand the cause of my death!” and was fitting the bonds to her pale neck.
sentences.i: She stands up, resolved to put her neck in a noose; and with her sash made fast to the top of the doorpost she said, “Goodbye, dear Cinyras — and understand why I die,” and began fitting the cord to her pale throat.
sentences.n: Erigitur is passive in form but reflexive in force, “she raises herself up.” innectere fauces takes the ablative laqueo, “to knot the throat with a noose.” zona ... revincta is an ablative absolute, “her sash having been tied fast,” with summo de poste, “from the top of the doorpost.” care ... Cinyra is a vocative: Cinyra is the vocative of the Greek-type first-declension name Cinyras. dixit is perfect and aptabat imperfect in the same sentence: the imperfect gives an action still going on when it is broken off, “she was fitting.” pallenti ... collo is a dative with aptabat, “to her pale neck.”

sentences.t:
Murmura verborum fidas nutricis ad aures
pervenisse ferunt limen servantis alumnae.
sentences.l: They report that the murmurs of her words came through to the faithful ears of the nurse, who was guarding her nursling's threshold.
sentences.i: The story goes that the murmur of her words reached the loyal ears of her nurse, who was keeping watch at her foster-child's door.
sentences.n: ferunt, “they say,” introduces the accusative and infinitive murmura ... pervenisse: the poet marks the tale as report, as the same verb marked hearsay in Myrrha's own mouth at line 331. servantis is a present participle in the genitive agreeing with nutricis, “of the nurse keeping watch,” and it takes limen alumnae as its own object. alumna is the girl the nurse reared, “nursling, foster-child.” fidas is held apart from its noun aures by nutricis ad, both words standing inside line 382, with aures closing the line.

sentences.t:
Surgit anus reseratque fores, mortisque paratae
instrumenta videns spatio conclamat eodem
seque ferit scinditque sinus ereptaque collo
vincula dilaniat.
sentences.l: The old woman rises and unbars the doors and, seeing the instruments of a death made ready, in that same moment she cries out, and strikes herself, and tears open her dress, and, with the bonds snatched from the neck, rips them to pieces.
sentences.i: The old woman gets up and unbolts the doors; and, seeing the equipment of a death already prepared, in that same instant she cries out, beats herself, tears her clothes open, snatches the cords from the girl's neck and rips them apart.
sentences.n: anus is the noun for an old woman, and it is the nurse. mortis ... paratae is a genitive with instrumenta, “the instruments of a death made ready.” spatio ... eodem is an ablative of time, “within that same interval,” i.e. all at once. The four verbs conclamat, ferit, scindit, dilaniat run on with -que and no pause, matching the rush of the action. erepta ... vincula is a participle attached to the object where English wants a second verb, “the bonds, snatched away,” with collo an ablative of separation, “from the neck.” Tearing open the folds of the dress is the standing Roman gesture of grief.

sentences.t:
Tum denique flere vacavit,
tum dare complexus laqueique requirere causam.
sentences.l: Then at last there was leisure to weep, then to give embraces and to seek out the reason for the noose.
sentences.i: Only then was there time to weep, and to embrace her, and to ask what the noose was for.
sentences.n: vacavit is impersonal, “there was free time,” with the infinitives flere, dare and requirere standing as its subject. The repeated tum ... tum marks the order of things: action first, feeling afterwards. complexus is a fourth-declension accusative plural, “embraces.” laquei is an objective genitive with causam, “the reason for the noose.”

sentences.t:
Muta silet virgo terramque inmota tuetur
et deprensa dolet tardae conamina mortis.
sentences.l: The girl is silent and dumb, and unmoving she gazes at the ground, and grieves over the caught-out attempts at a death too slow.
sentences.i: The girl keeps a dumb silence, stares at the ground without moving, and grieves that her attempt at a death too slow in coming has been found out.
sentences.n: Muta and inmota are nominative adjectives agreeing with virgo, doing work that English gives to adverbs — “dumb,” “without moving”; inmota keeps the edition's older unassimilated spelling for immota. deprensa is a perfect participle agreeing with conamina and carrying the weight of a whole clause, “the attempts, having been caught out.” tardae ... mortis is a genitive with conamina, “attempts at a slow death”; tardus is “late, slow in coming,” and the death has been made late by the rescue.

sentences.t:
Instat anus canosque suos et inania nudans
ubera per cunas alimentaque prima precatur,
ut sibi committat, quidquid dolet.
sentences.l: The old woman presses her hard and, laying bare her white hairs and her empty breasts, entreats her by the cradle and by the first feeding to entrust to her whatever she is grieving over.
sentences.i: The old woman presses her, and, uncovering her white hair and her empty breasts, begs her by the cradle and by the milk she first gave her to trust her with whatever is hurting her.
sentences.n: canos is the adjective canus used as a noun, “white hairs.” inania and ubera are split by nudans and by the line-end: inania stands next to last in line 391, with nudans after it, and ubera opens 392. precor per is the formula of solemn entreaty, “I beg you by,” and what the nurse swears by is her own past service — the cradle and the first feeding. ut ... committat is an indirect command with the subjunctive after precatur, “that she entrust.” quidquid dolet keeps doleo in its transitive use, “whatever she grieves over.”

sentences.t:
Illa rogantem
aversata gemit. Certa est exquirere nutrix
nec solam spondere fidem:
sentences.l: She turns away from the one asking and groans. The nurse is determined to search the thing out, and not merely to pledge her good faith:
sentences.i: She turns her face from the woman's asking and groans. The nurse is set on getting it out of her, and on more than a pledge of loyalty:
sentences.n: aversata is the perfect participle of the deponent aversor — passive in form, active in meaning, “having turned away from” — and it takes the accusative rogantem, itself a present participle used as a noun, “the woman asking.” Certa est with the infinitives exquirere and spondere is “she is resolved to.” solam attaches to fidem, “loyalty alone”: the point is that the nurse will not stop at pledging her loyalty, she means to act, and the colon leads straight into what she says.

sentences.t:
“dic” inquit “opemque
me sine ferre tibi; non est mea pigra senectus.
sentences.l: “Speak,” she says, “and allow me to bring you help; my old age is not sluggish.
sentences.i: “Tell me,” she says, “and let me help you: my old age is not a sluggish one.
sentences.n: sine is the imperative of sino, “allow,” with the accusative and infinitive me ... ferre, “allow me to bring.” inquit is dropped inside the quotation rather than placed before it, as Latin regularly does with verbs of saying. pigra is “slow, sluggish, good for nothing”: the nurse is answering an objection the girl has not made.

sentences.t:
Seu furor est, habeo, quae carmine sanet et herbis,
sive aliquis nocuit, magico lustrabere ritu,
ira deum sive est, sacris placabilis ira.
sentences.l: If it is madness, I have a woman to heal you with charm and with herbs; if someone has done you harm, you will be purified by a magic rite; if it is the anger of the gods, anger is appeasable by sacrifice.
sentences.i: If it is madness, I know a woman who can cure it with a spell and with herbs; if someone has put a harm on you, you will be cleansed by a magic rite; if it is the anger of the gods, anger can be appeased with sacrifice.
sentences.n: Three conditions in a row: seu ... sive ... sive, “whether ... or ... or.” habeo, quae ... sanet is a relative clause of purpose or characteristic with the subjunctive — “I have a woman to heal,” not “who heals”; quae is feminine, which is why the literal names a woman. carmen is a spell or incantation, the same word that stood for the poet's own song at line 301. lustrabere is a second-person future passive, an alternative for lustraberis, “you will be ritually cleansed.” deum is the shortened genitive plural for deorum. sacris is an ablative of means, “by rites,” and ira is repeated at the line's end so that the remedy stands beside the complaint.

sentences.t:
Quid rear ulterius ? Certe fortuna domusque
sospes et in cursu est, vivit genetrixque paterque.”
sentences.l: What further am I to suppose? Certainly your fortune and your house are safe and on their course; your mother lives, and your father.”
sentences.i: What else am I to think? Your fortunes and your household are surely safe and going well; your mother is alive, and your father.”
sentences.n: rear is a deliberative subjunctive of the deponent reor, “what am I to think?” — a genuine question about what to conclude, not a wish. sospes is a single predicate adjective doing duty for both fortuna and domus. vivit is singular although two subjects follow it, genetrix and pater, each with its own -que; the literal keeps the singular verb. The word the nurse ends on is pater, and it is the word that undoes the girl in the next line. One point of printing: the edition sets a space before the question mark in line 400, Quid rear ulterius ?, and we ship the line exactly as it stands there. The words are ordinary Latin and the sentence construes, so the spacing is all that is odd; nothing is claimed here about the metre.

sentences.t:
Myrrha, patre audito, suspiria duxit ab imo
pectore.
sentences.l: Myrrha, her father having been heard [named], drew sighs from the bottom of her breast.
sentences.i: At the word “father,” Myrrha drew sighs from the bottom of her breast.
sentences.n: patre audito is an ablative absolute, “her father having been heard,” that is, the word “father” having been spoken; “[named]” is supplied in the literal to show what it was she heard. imo ... pectore is an ablative of source with the superlative-form adjective imus, “the lowest part of the breast,” split across the line-end — imo closes line 402 and pectore opens 403. suspiria duxit is the ordinary phrase, “drew sighs.”

sentences.t:
Nec nutrix etiamnum concipit ullum
mente nefas, aliquemque tamen praesentit amorem;
sentences.l: Nor does the nurse conceive any abomination in her mind even now; yet she senses beforehand some love;
sentences.i: Even now the nurse does not imagine any horror; yet she does sense that there is some love in it;
sentences.n: concipit ... mente nefas answers the girl's own animo ne concipe at line 352: the nurse cannot conceive the thing Myrrha ordered herself not to conceive. ullum and nefas are split across the line-end — ullum closes line 403 and nefas stands second in 404, after mente. praesentit is “feels in advance, has a foreboding of,” with amorem as its object; aliquem is the indefinite, “some love or other,” which the nurse cannot yet name.

sentences.t:
propositique tenax, quodcumque est, orat, ut ipsi
indicet,
sentences.l: and, holding fast to her purpose — whatever it is — she begs that the girl tell it to her,
sentences.i: and, clinging to her purpose, whatever the trouble is, she begs the girl to tell her,
sentences.n: tenax takes the genitive, propositi, “holding fast to her purpose.” quodcumque est is parenthetic, “whatever it is” — the nurse does not know what she is asking for. ut ... indicet is an indirect command with the subjunctive after orat; ipsi is dative, and the ipse marks that it is to the nurse herself, in person, that the girl is to tell it. The subject changes inside the sentence: the nurse begs, the girl is to disclose.

sentences.t:
et gremio lacrimantem tollit anili
atque ita complectens infirmis membra lacertis
“sensimus,” inquit “amas!
sentences.l: and lifts the weeping girl into her aged lap, and, embracing her limbs so with feeble arms, she says: “We have realised it — you are in love!
sentences.i: and lifts the weeping girl into her old lap; and, holding her so in her weak arms, she says: “I have seen it — you are in love!
sentences.n: gremio and anili, “an old woman's lap,” are held apart by lacrimantem tollit, both inside line 406, with anili closing the line. lacrimantem is a present participle used as a noun, “the weeping one.” sensimus is a perfect of realisation — “it has come home to me” — and the first person plural stands for the singular, a common poetic usage: the literal keeps the plural, the idiomatic makes it singular. infirmis ... lacertis is an ablative of means, “with feeble arms.”

sentences.t:
sed et hic mea (pone timorem)
sedulitas erit apta tibi, nec sentiet umquam
hoc pater.”
sentences.l: but here too my attentive service — lay aside your fear — will be fitted to your need, and your father will never perceive this.”
sentences.i: but in this too my devotion — set your fear aside — will serve you, and your father will never come to know of it.”
sentences.n: mea and sedulitas, “my attentive service,” are split by the parenthesis and the line-end: mea stands late in line 408 with the aside (pone timorem) after it, and sedulitas opens 409. pone timorem is an imperative dropped into the middle of the sentence as an aside. apta takes the dative tibi, “fitted to you, equal to your need.” hic is the adverb, “in this matter.” hoc is the neuter object of sentiet, “will perceive this.” The nurse binds herself to help before she has been told what she is helping with.

sentences.t:
Exsiluit gremio furibunda torumque
ore premens “discede, precor, miseroque pudori
parce!” ait.
sentences.l: She leapt out of the lap in a frenzy and, pressing the couch with her face, says: “Go away, I beg, and spare my wretched shame!”
sentences.i: She sprang out of the old woman's lap in a frenzy and, burying her face in the couch, says: “Go away, I beg you — spare my miserable shame!”
sentences.n: Exsiluit is perfect, “she leapt out,” with gremio an ablative of separation, “out of the lap”; ait beside it is present, the tense alternation that runs through this part, and both layers keep it. furibunda is a nominative adjective agreeing with the unnamed subject, “raving,” doing the work of an English adverb. torum is split from its participle premens by the line-end — torumque closes line 410 and ore premens opens 411. parce takes the dative, misero ... pudori, “spare my wretched shame.”

sentences.t:
Instanti “discede, aut desine” dixit
“quaerere, quid doleam: scelus est, quod scire laboras.”
sentences.l: To her as she pressed on she said: “Go away — or stop asking what I grieve over: it is a crime, the thing you are labouring to know.”
sentences.i: To the nurse, still pressing her, she said, “Go away — or stop asking what my grief is. What you are working so hard to learn is a crime.”
sentences.n: Instanti is the dative of a present participle used as a noun, “to the woman pressing on,” naming the person spoken to. desine takes the infinitive quaerere, and the two are separated by the line-end and by the intervening dixit — desine stands late in line 412, with dixit after it, and quaerere opens 413. quid doleam is an indirect question with the subjunctive, “what I grieve over.” quod scire laboras is the clause standing as subject of scelus est, “what you are labouring to know is a crime,” and the girl names her own case with the same word the poet used of it at line 314.
